01Fig. 1

Where the work waits

Hand-built identity-specimens/d-drawn/index.html

Work flows from Ideas through Refinement, Development and Review to Release. The longest queue sits in front of Review, where 14 changes wait for one senior reviewer. Development has 9 changes in progress for 5 developers. Adding developers increases the review queue; the constraint is review capacity.

Rendered figures/fig1.ts

A team of 5 developers and 1 senior reviewer has 14 changes waiting for review.

Add 2 developers and 22 changes wait.

Illustrative model: each developer finishes four changes a week, one senior reviewer clears six. The figure shows one week.

02Fig. 2

Two ways to work with agents

Hand-built identity-specimens/d-drawn/index.html

In the fleet workflow, a large plan is split into tasks and sent to agents in separate workspaces; code appears quickly and a dashboard shows activity, but understanding is lost. In the current workflow, one groomed issue becomes one small task, worked in a worktree by an orchestrator, an implementer and a reviewer, then crosses as a pull request into Martin's review before it is merged. The constraint is Martin's review, by design.

03Fig. 3

The bottleneck moves

Rendered figures/fig3.ts

Before: Work flows from Ideas through Refinement, Development and Review to Release. Ideas has 48 waiting, unlimited capacity. Refinement has 12 waiting for 1 product owner. Development has 9 in progress for 5 developers. Review has 14 waiting for 1 senior reviewer. Release has none waiting, capacity every 2 weeks. The constraint is Review, 1 senior reviewer. After a second reviewer: Review has 3 waiting with 2 senior reviewers and Release has 11 waiting; the constraint moves to Release, every 2 weeks.

// Derived from Martin's brief "What Factorio taught me about agile bottlenecks":
// "approval layers and dependencies become invisible queues", "bottlenecks move, but rituals stay fixed".

  id: "fig-3", number: 3, title: "The bottleneck moves", note: "Numbers are illustrative.",
